clinicalPearls: A classic cause of acute nephritic syndrome in children, most often between about 5 and 12 years of age.
Follows infection with specific nephritogenic strains of group A streptococcus, typically 1-2 weeks after pharyngitis or 3-6 weeks after skin infection.
Presents with the nephritic picture of haematuria (often cola- or tea-coloured urine), oedema, hypertension, and variable reduction in urine output.
Complement C3 is characteristically low and typically returns to normal within about 6-8 weeks; persistently low C3 beyond this window suggests another diagnosis.
Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection is supported by elevated or rising antistreptococcal antibodies such as ASO or anti-DNase B.
Management is largely supportive, centred on salt and fluid restriction and control of hypertension and fluid overload.
Antibiotics treat any active streptococcal infection but do not alter the course of the established nephritis.
Renal biopsy is usually unnecessary and reserved for atypical features such as persistent low complement, progressive kidney failure, or nephrotic-range proteinuria.
The prognosis in children is excellent, with the large majority recovering complete renal function.
reference.pathophysiology: Infection with nephritogenic strains of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus triggers an immune-complex-mediated glomerular injury. Streptococcal antigens (such as nephritis-associated plasmin receptor and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B) deposit in the glomeruli and, together with circulating and in situ immune complexes, activate the complement system, predominantly via the alternative pathway. The resulting inflammation causes endocapillary proliferation and neutrophil infiltration, reducing glomerular filtration and producing sodium and water retention, which manifests as haematuria, oedema, and hypertension.
additionalDifferentials: Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease
additionalInvestigations: Serum complement C3 (and C4) with follow-up to document normalisation
Antistreptococcal serology (ASO, anti-DNase B) or streptozyme panel
Throat or skin swab and culture if active infection present
Urinalysis with microscopy for red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells
Serum urea, creatinine, and electrolytes to assess renal function
Renal biopsy only in atypical or progressive cases
redFlags: Severe or refractory hypertension, including hypertensive encephalopathy
Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Pulmonary oedema or heart failure from fluid overload
Persistently low complement or nephrotic-range proteinuria indicating an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Most children recover fully; acute complications resolve over days to weeks, complement normalises within about two months, and microscopic haematuria may persist for up to a year with an excellent long-term outlook.
pitfalls: Attributing every child with haematuria and low C3 to PSGN without follow-up complement testing
Overlooking hypertensive complications by not monitoring blood pressure closely
Failing to consider alternative glomerulonephritides when complement stays low beyond eight weeks
Aggressive fluid administration worsening volume overload in an oliguric child
